subtopic_detail: Moderate ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome outpatient vs inpatient management
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 31 year old woman in the emergency department 6 days after a fresh embryo transfer following a gonadotrophin cycle. She has abdominal distension, nausea, some vomiting and reduced urine output over the last day. She has no chest pain and no leg swelling. She has had two large volume fluids over the past 24 hours. Her pain is manageable with paracetamol.

Her weight is 4 kg above baseline. She is tolerating oral fluids in small amounts between vomits. Her most recent transabdominal ultrasound shows bilateral ovaries measuring 9 cm each, moderate free fluid in the pouch of Douglas, no pleural effusion visible. Her home is 30 minutes from the tertiary hospital and she lives with her partner.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen with generalised tenderness, no peritonism, bowel sounds present, mild dyspnoea when supine
data_table.Investigations: Haematocrit 0.44 L/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 74 micromol/L, white cell count 8.4 x10^9/L, beta hCG 210 IU/L

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management plan now?

options.text: Discharge with oral fluid guide, daily weight, daily urine output diary and same next day gynaecology review
options.rationale: This is moderate ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome with weight gain <5 kg, haematocrit <0.45 L/L, normal renal function, adequate oral intake, no pleural effusion or thromboembolism and a stable social situation; outpatient management with structured monitoring is appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

options.text: Admit for intravenous 0.9 percent saline at 200 mL/hour and diagnostic paracentesis of the pouch of Douglas fluid
options.rationale: Paracentesis is reserved for severe or critical ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome with respiratory compromise, tense ascites, or oliguria refractory to conservative therapy. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

options.text: Admit for intravenous 25 percent albumin infusion and dopamine renal dose for prevention of oliguric renal injury
options.rationale: Neither high dose albumin nor dopamine renal dose are supported for prevention of renal injury in ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome and both add risk. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

options.text: Admit for empirical broad spectrum antibiotics for possible ovarian abscess complicating this stimulation cycle
options.rationale: Ovarian abscess is not a routine consideration in this scenario; markers are not consistent with sepsis and empirical antibiotics are not indicated. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

options.text: Admit for immediate laparoscopy to detorse and possibly resect the enlarged ovaries prior to further deterioration
options.rationale: Ovarian torsion is a specific surgical emergency with characteristic pain, and prophylactic surgery of hyperstimulated ovaries is contraindicated because they are friable. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

explanation.summary: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome is graded by symptoms, haemoconcentration, ascites, renal function and thromboembolic markers. Moderate cases with haematocrit under 0.45 L/L, weight gain under 5 kg, adequate urine output, ability to tolerate oral fluids and stable social supports can be managed as outpatients with a daily weight and urine diary, thromboprophylaxis in high risk cases and a same next day review. Admission is reserved for severe features (haematocrit >=0.45 L/L, oliguria, pleural effusion, hyponatraemia, coagulopathy). Paracentesis, albumin infusion and prophylactic surgery are all reserved for specific severe scenarios.
key_points: Moderate ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (haematocrit <0.45, urine output preserved) can be managed as outpatient with structured monitoring.
Severe features prompt admission: haematocrit >=0.45, oliguria, pleural effusion, coagulopathy, tense ascites.
Prophylactic laparoscopy of hyperstimulated ovaries is contraindicated because they are friable.
explanation.pearls: A moderate ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome with haematocrit 0.44 L/L, tolerating oral fluid and preserved urine output goes home with a monitoring diary and next day review.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome
ESHRE Ovarian Stimulation Guideline

subtopic_detail: Second line uterotonic choice with hypertensive contraindication
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar in the birth suite immediately after the vaginal delivery of a 3.9 kg live infant to a 34 year old woman. Third stage was actively managed with prophylactic oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly. The placenta appears complete at 8 minutes with no obvious retained tissue. Over 5 minutes there is a rapid trickle of blood, estimated blood loss 850 mL, and the uterus is boggy. A syntocinon infusion 40 units in 1 L 0.9 percent saline has been commenced running at 250 mL/hour. Bimanual compression is being performed by the senior midwife. The estimated blood loss continues to rise.

Her antenatal record shows two clinic readings of 158/98 mmHg and 156/94 mmHg during the third trimester and she is currently on labetalol 200 mg twice daily for gestational hypertension. She has no asthma, no cardiac disease, no known contraindication to prostaglandins. Repeat blood pressure 3 minutes ago was 154/96 mmHg. Placenta reviewed and complete.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116 /min, blood pressure 152/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Examination: Uterus boggy 22 weeks size, rising fundus, bimanual compression in progress, no visible cervical or perineal tear on inspection
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin pre-labour 110 g/L (115-165), platelets 220 x10^9/L, fibrinogen not yet available; group O positive

lead_in: Which second line uterotonic is most appropriate now?

options.text: Intramuscular ergometrine 250 microg with intravenous metoclopramide 10 mg antiemetic cover given now for the acute bleed
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and pre eclampsia because of ergot mediated vasoconstriction and severe hypertensive crisis risk; her blood pressure and gestational hypertension exclude this. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.text: Intramuscular carboprost 250 microg (15 methyl prostaglandin F2 alpha) now, repeat at 15 minutes if bleeding continues
options.rationale: Carboprost is the appropriate second line uterotonic when ergometrine is contraindicated by hypertension; it can be repeated every 15 minutes up to a total of 2 mg with asthma being the main contraindication to consider. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.text: Rectal misoprostol 800 microg alone as the next uterotonic agent and hold further parenteral agents at this time
options.rationale: Misoprostol may be used but has slow onset and is less effective as monotherapy in ongoing bleeding; parenteral carboprost is preferred when available in ongoing haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.text: Repeat intramuscular oxytocin 10 units now and observe for 15 minutes before further uterotonic escalation this bleed
options.rationale: Repeating oxytocin in a woman already on an oxytocin infusion at 250 mL/hour with ongoing haemorrhage is not the next step; escalate to a different uterotonic mechanism. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.text: Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate 200 microg now to relax the uterus and allow prompt manual removal in this bleed
options.rationale: Glyceryl trinitrate is a uterine relaxant used for a trapped placenta or uterine inversion, not for atonic bleeding after a complete placenta. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage

explanation.summary: Atonic postpartum haemorrhage after adequate oxytocin needs a different uterotonic mechanism. Ergometrine causes ergot mediated vasoconstriction and precipitates hypertensive crisis in women with pre eclampsia or hypertension. Carboprost (15 methyl prostaglandin F2 alpha) is the preferred second line agent when ergometrine is contraindicated; the main contraindication for carboprost itself is asthma. Misoprostol 800 microg rectally is an option in low resource settings or where parenteral prostaglandin is unavailable. Concurrent tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous is standard adjunct in postpartum haemorrhage.
key_points: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and pre eclampsia.
Carboprost 250 microg intramuscularly, repeat every 15 minutes to 2 mg total, asthma is the main contraindication.
Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous is a standard adjunct in postpartum haemorrhage.
explanation.pearls: A woman with gestational hypertension and ongoing atonic postpartum haemorrhage gets carboprost as the second line uterotonic, not ergometrine.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage
Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: Uterotonics

subtopic_detail: Vasa praevia identification and delivery timing
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar reviewing a 32 year old primigravida at 32 weeks gestation in the high risk clinic. The morphology scan at 20 weeks had noted a bilobed placenta and a low lying placenta 22 mm from the internal os, and a follow up transvaginal scan at 30 weeks was arranged. That scan showed the placenta 40 mm from the os but visualised unprotected foetal vessels crossing the internal os anteriorly. Colour Doppler confirmed foetal arterial waveform on the vessels traversing the os. The rest of the pregnancy has been uncomplicated with normal glucose tolerance test.

She reports no bleeding and normal foetal movements. She lives 40 minutes from the tertiary maternity unit. She and her partner ask about the plan for the rest of the pregnancy and birth. Antenatal corticosteroids have not been given.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Symphysial fundal height 31 cm, foetal heart 148 /min, no palpable contractions, no vaginal bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound 30 weeks: bilobed placenta, placenta clear of the internal os but unprotected foetal vessels crossing the os with foetal arterial Doppler; foetal growth 40th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Serial growth scans and planned vaginal birth at 40 weeks with expectant management if labour begins spontaneously
options.rationale: Vaginal birth is contraindicated in vasa praevia because rupture of membranes can precipitate foetal exsanguination; delivery must be by planned caesarean before labour. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia

options.text: Immediate caesarean this week at 32 weeks gestation with antenatal corticosteroid loading given intrapartum only
options.rationale: 32 weeks is too early to deliver an asymptomatic woman with vasa praevia and no evidence of bleeding or labour; corticosteroids given intrapartum are too late for maximal benefit. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia

options.text: Admit at 32 to 34 weeks for antenatal corticosteroids and inpatient monitoring, plan elective caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks
options.rationale: RANZCOG recommends antenatal corticosteroids at 32 to 34 weeks, inpatient monitoring (particularly for women living far from a maternity unit) and planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks to balance prematurity against catastrophic haemorrhage from ruptured foetal vessels at membrane rupture. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia

options.text: Outpatient management until 39 weeks with a caesarean planned then if she has not laboured spontaneously by that date
options.rationale: Planned caesarean at 39 weeks carries an unacceptable risk of spontaneous rupture of membranes and foetal exsanguination in the interval; delivery must be planned before labour. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia

options.text: Weekly cardiotocograph plus vaginal ultrasound reassessment, delivery only when foetal vessels move clear of the os
options.rationale: Foetal vessels overlying the internal os do not resolve reliably and expectant management delays needed delivery; planned early caesarean is the intervention. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia is characterised by unprotected foetal vessels traversing or lying close to the internal cervical os. Membrane rupture with these vessels present precipitates foetal exsanguination within minutes. Australian guidance recommends antenatal corticosteroids at 32 to 34 weeks, inpatient admission where the woman lives at a distance from a maternity unit, and planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks to balance prematurity risk against catastrophic haemorrhage risk. Vaginal birth is contraindicated. Suspicion is triggered on morphology scan features such as bilobed placenta, low lying placenta or velamentous cord insertion, then confirmed on transvaginal colour Doppler.
key_points: Vasa praevia risk factors: bilobed placenta, low lying placenta, velamentous cord insertion.
Vaginal birth contraindicated; deliver by planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids.
Consider inpatient admission from 32 weeks if geography or bleeding raises risk.
explanation.pearls: Vasa praevia is delivered by planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids at 32 to 34 weeks, not at term.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia
SMFM Consult Series 37: Diagnosis and management of vasa previa

subtopic_detail: Magnesium sulfate toxicity clinical assessment vs level
stem:
You are the obstetrics and gynaecology registrar overnight on the birth suite. A 27 year old primigravida at 35 weeks with severe pre eclampsia had a loading dose of magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenous over 20 minutes 3 hours ago, followed by a maintenance infusion at 1 g/hour. Blood pressure is now under 155/95 mmHg with intravenous labetalol. She had a witnessed eclamptic seizure earlier this shift. She is under continuous cardiotocograph. Urine output has been 25 mL in the last hour, having previously been 40 to 60 mL/hour. Her most recent creatinine was 88 micromol/L.

On assessment she is drowsier than 2 hours ago. Her deep tendon reflexes are absent at the patellae and biceps. Her respiratory rate has fallen. Foetal heart is 138 /min with normal variability. Repeat magnesium levels have been sent but the result is not yet available. Calcium gluconate is available in the emergency drug drawer.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 /min, blood pressure 150/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 10 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, absent patellar and biceps reflexes, no muscle fasciculation, no jaundice, foetal heart 138 /min normal variability
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 88 micromol/L, platelets 92 x10^9/L, alanine transaminase 62 U/L, magnesium level pending; urine output 25 mL in last hour

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Increase magnesium sulfate infusion to 2 g/hour empirically for possible seizure recurrence, reduce blood pressure to 130/80 mmHg
options.rationale: The clinical picture is magnesium toxicity, not seizure recurrence; increasing the infusion worsens toxicity, and aggressive blood pressure reduction below 140/90 risks foetal compromise. (Source: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy)
source_refs: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

options.text: Continue infusion at current rate pending the pending magnesium level, review clinical status in one hour with midwifery
options.rationale: Waiting for a level in the face of areflexia, respiratory depression and oliguria risks respiratory arrest; clinical toxicity mandates action before the level returns. (Source: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy)
source_refs: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

options.text: Give intravenous furosemide 40 mg to induce diuresis to clear magnesium faster and reduce accumulation of drug
options.rationale: Loop diuresis carries risk of hypotension and does not immediately antagonise the neuromuscular effect; calcium gluconate is the antagonist to give during clinical toxicity. (Source: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy)
source_refs: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

options.text: Stop magnesium sulfate, give intravenous calcium gluconate 1 g over 10 minutes, support ventilation, reassess reflexes hourly
options.rationale: Loss of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory depression and reduced urine output are clinical signs of magnesium toxicity; the appropriate step is to stop the infusion, give calcium gluconate 1 g over 10 minutes as an antagonist, and support respiration and monitor closely without waiting for the level. (Source: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy)
source_refs: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

options.text: Administer intravenous diazepam 5 mg as an anticonvulsant substitute and continue magnesium sulfate at a reduced rate
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are second line for magnesium refractory seizures; here the clinical problem is magnesium toxicity not seizure and diazepam risks compound respiratory depression. (Source: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy)
source_refs: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

explanation.summary: Magnesium toxicity in a pre eclamptic woman on magnesium sulfate is a clinical diagnosis: loss of patellar reflexes, reduced respiratory rate, drowsiness and oliguria all indicate rising levels. Because renal clearance dominates elimination, oliguria drives accumulation. The clinical assessment does not wait for the level; the infusion is stopped and intravenous calcium gluconate 1 g over 10 minutes antagonises the neuromuscular effect. Ventilatory support is added if respiration is compromised. Once stable the infusion may be recommenced at a lower rate with closer monitoring and dose adjustment for renal function.
key_points: Magnesium toxicity is clinical: absent reflexes, respiratory depression, oliguria.
Antidote is calcium gluconate 1 g intravenous over 10 minutes; stop the infusion first.
Oliguria drives accumulation; adjust the rate for reduced renal clearance.
explanation.pearls: Absent patellar reflexes and respiratory rate 10 /min on magnesium sulfate is toxicity: stop the infusion and give calcium gluconate 1 g intravenous over 10 minutes.

sources.label: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: Magnesium sulfate in pre eclampsia

subtopic_detail: Amniotic fluid embolism with cardiorespiratory collapse and disseminated intravascular coagulation
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite of a tertiary hospital. A 38 year old woman had spontaneous rupture of membranes 5 minutes ago in the second stage of labour. Immediately after rupture she became agitated, then unresponsive with sudden hypoxaemia and hypotension. She is now intubated and receiving cardiopulmonary resuscitation with return of spontaneous circulation after 4 minutes. Immediate perimortem caesarean birth was performed at 5 minutes; foetus is transferred to the resuscitaire. The uterus is boggy with a large amount of ongoing dark and clotting-poor vaginal bleeding and generalised oozing from the venepuncture sites and around the endotracheal tube.

Massive transfusion protocol has been activated. First red cells and fresh frozen plasma are hanging. Tranexamic acid 1 g is running. Anaesthetics and intensive care are attending. The next set of coagulation results has just arrived and are markedly abnormal. Cardiac output has been restored on noradrenaline 20 microg/min.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, blood pressure 88/48 mmHg on noradrenaline, respiratory rate mechanical, SpO2 92% on FiO2 1.0, temperature 36.0 degC
data_table.Examination: Boggy uterus, ongoing vaginal bleeding, oozing venepuncture sites, bilateral bibasal crackles on chest auscultation, no visible perineal laceration
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 62 g/L (115-165), platelets 42 x10^9/L, fibrinogen 0.8 g/L (2.0-4.0), INR 2.8, activated partial thromboplastin time 78 s, D dimer >20 mg/L, arterial pH 7.10 lactate 8 mmol/L

lead_in: In addition to ongoing red cells and fresh frozen plasma, which single next intervention is most likely to reduce mortality?

options.text: Recombinant activated factor VII 90 microg/kg intravenous bolus as a haemostatic agent to control bleeding rapidly now
options.rationale: Recombinant activated factor VII is not first line in amniotic fluid embolism and has an increased thrombotic and pulmonary vascular complication risk in this setting; correction of fibrinogen and platelets and empirical haemostatic products come first. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism

options.text: Continuous cell salvage from the surgical field with re infusion to reduce donor red cell exposure through this bleed
options.rationale: Cell salvage is a useful adjunct in obstetric haemorrhage but does not correct the coagulopathy and does not treat the pulmonary vasoconstrictive component of amniotic fluid embolism; it is not the priority. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism

options.text: Intravenous ergometrine 500 microg immediately to reverse uterine atony contributing to the ongoing haemorrhage
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in this haemodynamic and pulmonary state; the pulmonary vasoconstriction would worsen right ventricular failure. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism

options.text: Intravenous heparin 5000 unit bolus to address the disseminated intravascular coagulation contributing to this bleed
options.rationale: Anticoagulation would worsen active haemorrhage and is not indicated in amniotic fluid embolism related disseminated intravascular coagulation which is predominantly consumptive and fibrinolytic. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism

options.text: Cryoprecipitate 10 units targeted to fibrinogen above 2 g/L with concurrent platelets to keep platelets above 50
options.rationale: Fibrinogen falls first and fastest in amniotic fluid embolism related consumptive coagulopathy; targeted cryoprecipitate to fibrinogen above 2 g/L reduces mortality more than fresh frozen plasma alone at low fibrinogen. Concurrent platelets are kept above 50 x10^9/L in the actively bleeding patient. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism has three overlapping phases: sudden cardiopulmonary collapse from pulmonary vasoconstriction and right ventricular failure, hypoxia and neurological dysfunction, and consumptive coagulopathy with a marked and early drop in fibrinogen. Management is supportive: airway and ventilation, haemodynamic support with noradrenaline and consideration of pulmonary vasodilators or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and aggressive correction of coagulopathy targeting fibrinogen above 2 g/L with cryoprecipitate and platelets above 50 x10^9/L. Ergometrine, heparin and recombinant activated factor VII are variously contraindicated or unproven; the primary haemostatic priority is fibrinogen replacement.
key_points: Amniotic fluid embolism coagulopathy is fibrinogen consumption first; cryoprecipitate to keep fibrinogen above 2 g/L.
Ergometrine is contraindicated because of pulmonary vasoconstriction risk.
Anticoagulation is not indicated during active haemorrhage from amniotic fluid embolism related disseminated intravascular coagulation.
explanation.pearls: In amniotic fluid embolism with fibrinogen 0.8 g/L, cryoprecipitate targeted to above 2 g/L is the survival step; do not give ergometrine, heparin or recombinant activated factor VII.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism
National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guideline Module 5 Obstetrics

subtopic_detail: Fitness to drive when starting stimulant treatment
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 28 year old woman with a recent diagnosis of adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder by a psychiatrist. She has moderate to severe symptoms with impaired concentration at work as a data analyst and difficulty organising study for a professional exam. She has an unrestricted private driver licence and drives 30 minutes to work daily. She is due to start methylphenidate extended release under a shared care arrangement with the psychiatrist. She has no seizure history, no cardiac disease and normal blood pressure at 118/74 mmHg.

She asks whether she can continue to drive during the initiation period. She has not had any recent motor vehicle crash and holds no commercial licence.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 /min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, no tremor, no thought disorder, unremarkable cardiovascular examination
data_table.Investigations: Baseline electrocardiogram sinus rhythm 74 /min, thyroid function normal, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about driving under the AU Assessing Fitness to Drive standard?

options.text: Continue driving her private vehicle while ADHD is treated and stable, with duty to self report medication adverse effects
options.rationale: The Assessing Fitness to Drive private licence standard allows driving when ADHD is under treatment and stable; the driver has a duty to self report any adverse effect of medication (sedation, poor concentration, treatment interruption) that may impair driving. (Source: Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022 Austroads)
source_refs: Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022 Austroads

options.text: Surrender her private licence for a minimum of 6 months from the day of diagnosis regardless of any treatment response
options.rationale: Automatic surrender is not part of the standard for a private licence when the condition is under treatment and stable. (Source: Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022 Austroads)
source_refs: Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022 Austroads

options.text: Barred from private driving until she has completed a 6 monthly cognitive testing battery with a neuropsychologist
options.rationale: Neuropsychological testing is not routinely required for private licence retention in stable treated ADHD. (Source: Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022 Austroads)
source_refs: Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022 Austroads

options.text: Switch to a commercial licence pathway and follow more frequent review criteria before returning to any driving
options.rationale: Commercial licence pathway is stricter and is required for commercial licence holders, not for a private licence in an office worker. (Source: Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022 Austroads)
source_refs: Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022 Austroads

options.text: Because methylphenidate is a schedule 8 stimulant she must not drive at any time on it regardless of stability
options.rationale: Schedule 8 status alone does not preclude driving; stability of the condition and absence of impairment govern private licence retention. (Source: Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022 Austroads)
source_refs: Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022 Austroads

explanation.summary: Under the Australian Assessing Fitness to Drive standard, adult ADHD is compatible with an unrestricted private licence provided the condition is under treatment and the driver is stable. The driver has an ongoing duty to self report any factor that could impair driving, including adverse effect of medication, sedation from titration, discontinuation, or comorbid substance use. Commercial licence holders and vocational drivers face stricter requirements including more frequent review and a specialist opinion. Stimulant treatment (methylphenidate, dexamphetamine, lisdexamfetamine) does not itself preclude driving on the private standard when the condition is stable.
key_points: Private licence: ADHD stable and treated is compatible with driving; ongoing duty to self report.
Commercial licence: stricter, specialist opinion required.
Stimulant treatment does not on its own preclude driving on the private standard.
explanation.pearls: Stable treated adult ADHD is a private licence go under Assessing Fitness to Drive, with a duty to self report any medication adverse effect that impairs driving.

sources.label: Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022 Austroads
RACGP Adult ADHD guideline 2022

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy choice in a patient with depression
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 45 year old man who has been smoking 20 cigarettes daily for 25 years. He wants to quit and has tried nicotine patches alone twice for 4 weeks each with relapse in the second week both times. He has moderate depression currently controlled on sertraline 100 mg daily with a Kessler 10 score of 18. There is no history of self harm, psychotic symptoms or bipolar disorder. He has no seizure history. He is not on any other medication. Cardiovascular examination is normal. He has no gastrointestinal disease and no renal impairment.

He asks whether varenicline is safe for someone with depression, having heard mixed information from friends. He is motivated to try a different medication approach this time.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, euthymic today, no thought disorder, no psychomotor slowing
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function tests and urea and electrolytes within normal limits; carbon monoxide breath 22 parts per million

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacotherapy option now?

options.text: Nicotine patch 21 mg daily alone for a third attempt with a slower taper this time over an extended 12 week period
options.rationale: Repeated monotherapy patches at the same dose are unlikely to succeed after two failed attempts; combination or a different first line agent gives higher quit rates. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation 2021)
source_refs: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation 2021

options.text: Varenicline titrated over 1 week and continued for 12 weeks, with counselling on mood and sleep monitoring throughout
options.rationale: Varenicline gives the highest quit rate of the pharmacotherapy options and is not contraindicated in stable depression; large trials (EAGLES) did not find increased neuropsychiatric adverse events in stable depression compared with placebo, patch or bupropion. Standard titration and 12 week course plus monitoring for mood or sleep changes are recommended. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation 2021)
source_refs: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation 2021

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg daily added to sertraline for a combined effect on mood and craving over the coming quit attempt
options.rationale: Combining bupropion with sertraline increases seizure risk and serotonergic risk; bupropion is a reasonable option when antidepressant use is not present or is being switched, not co prescribed. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation 2021)
source_refs: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation 2021

options.text: Nortriptyline titrated up to 75 mg daily as an off label option for smoking cessation over the coming quit attempt
options.rationale: Nortriptyline is a second line option only, has anticholinergic and cardiovascular adverse effects, and combining with sertraline raises serotonergic risk; not first line in this scenario. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation 2021)
source_refs: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation 2021

options.text: Electronic cigarette (nicotine vaping product) prescribed under the current AU scheduling framework as a first line option
options.rationale: Nicotine vaping products are a second line option in AU only after registered pharmacotherapies have failed; they are not first line and require prescriber consideration of harm profile. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation 2021)
source_refs: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation 2021

explanation.summary: First line smoking cessation pharmacotherapies in Australia are varenicline, combination nicotine replacement therapy (patch plus faster acting form) and bupropion; nortriptyline is second line and nicotine vaping products are second line only after failed registered pharmacotherapy. Varenicline has the highest quit rate and is not contraindicated in stable depression; EAGLES did not find increased neuropsychiatric adverse events versus placebo in stable psychiatric populations. Monitoring for mood and sleep changes is still advisable. Co prescribing bupropion with a serotonergic antidepressant raises seizure and serotonergic risk. Combined nicotine replacement therapy would also be reasonable but varenicline is superior to any single option.
key_points: First line: varenicline, combination nicotine replacement therapy, or bupropion.
Varenicline is not contraindicated in stable depression (EAGLES data).
Nicotine vaping products are second line only after failure of registered agents.
explanation.pearls: Stable depression on sertraline does not exclude varenicline; it gives the highest quit rate and remains first line, with monitoring for mood and sleep.

Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Smoking cessation

stem:
You are the community psychiatry registrar reviewing a 42 year old woman with bipolar affective disorder type I. She has been stable on lithium carbonate 900 mg nocte for 3 years, most recently steady state trough level 0.7 mmol/L on 12 hour post dose sample. Her mood is euthymic today. She is asymptomatic. She reports no polyuria, no weight change, no cognitive dulling and no tremor.

Her last comprehensive monitoring bloods were taken 12 months ago. She has never had renal, thyroid or parathyroid disease. She takes no other prescribed medication. She lives independently and works in a public library. She asks what routine monitoring she should have now given the yearly review is due.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 /min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, euthymic, no fine tremor, no thyroid enlargement, no periorbital oedema
data_table.Investigations: Trough lithium 0.7 mmol/L 3 months ago; other bloods 12 months ago all normal

lead_in: Which monitoring panel best matches Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic recommendations for stable long term lithium therapy?

options.text: Lithium level every 6 months and full blood count every 6 months only, no other bloods routinely required in stable therapy
options.rationale: Full blood count is not part of routine lithium monitoring; renal, thyroid, calcium and lithium level are. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic Bipolar disorder)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic Bipolar disorder

options.text: Electrocardiogram every 6 months and weight only, no bloods needed at these routine reviews in stable long term therapy
options.rationale: Weight and blood pressure are useful but bloods are essential in long term lithium; routine electrocardiogram is not scheduled 6 monthly. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic Bipolar disorder)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic Bipolar disorder

options.text: Lithium level, urea and electrolytes with estimated glomerular filtration rate, thyroid stimulating hormone and calcium every 6 to 12 months
options.rationale: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic recommends lithium level, urea and electrolytes with estimated glomerular filtration rate, thyroid stimulating hormone and corrected calcium every 6 to 12 months in stable patients, plus weight and blood pressure at each review to monitor for lithium induced diabetes insipidus, chronic kidney disease, hypothyroidism and hyperparathyroidism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic Bipolar disorder)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic Bipolar disorder

options.text: Vitamin D and iron studies annually with a lithium level every 3 months, thyroid stimulating hormone every 2 years only
options.rationale: Vitamin D and iron studies are not part of routine lithium monitoring; thyroid stimulating hormone every 6 to 12 months not every 2 years. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic Bipolar disorder)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic Bipolar disorder

options.text: Fasting lipid panel and haemoglobin A1c every 6 months only because lithium is known to be associated with weight gain
options.rationale: Metabolic monitoring is important on some antipsychotics; lithium monitoring focuses on renal, thyroid, calcium and drug level. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic Bipolar disorder)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic Bipolar disorder

explanation.summary: Lithium requires ongoing monitoring for chronic kidney disease, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, hypothyroidism and hyperparathyroidism. In a stable patient, Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic recommends lithium level, urea and electrolytes with estimated glomerular filtration rate, thyroid stimulating hormone and corrected calcium every 6 to 12 months, plus weight and blood pressure at each review. More frequent testing follows dose change, illness, dehydration, non steroidal use or angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor introduction. Full blood count and vitamin D are not part of routine lithium monitoring, and routine electrocardiogram is not required outside baseline unless the patient has cardiac disease.
key_points: Every 6 to 12 months on stable lithium: level, urea and electrolytes with estimated glomerular filtration rate, thyroid stimulating hormone, corrected calcium.
At each review: weight and blood pressure.
More frequent testing after dose change, illness, non steroidal use, or angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor commencement.
explanation.pearls: Stable long term lithium: level, renal (with estimated glomerular filtration rate), thyroid stimulating hormone and calcium every 6 to 12 months plus weight and blood pressure at every visit.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic Bipolar disorder
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders 2020

subtopic_detail: First line approach for borderline personality disorder without prominent comorbidity
stem:
You are the community mental health team registrar seeing a 24 year old woman referred by her general practitioner for recurrent self harm and relationship distress. She meets criteria for borderline personality disorder with pattern of unstable relationships, chronic emptiness, non suicidal self injury with superficial forearm cutting, transient stress related paranoia and impulsivity around spending and alcohol binges. She has no current major depressive episode, no current substance use disorder, no eating disorder and no post traumatic stress disorder in remission. She works part time and has stable housing with her mother.

She has previously been trialled on citalopram 20 mg for a year with no clear benefit. She has never had structured psychological therapy. There is no history of psychosis. She is engaged and asking what help is available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 116/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, dysphoric with reactive mood, thought form goal directed, no psychotic phenomena, healed superficial scars on both forearms
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function, full blood count, urea and electrolytes and liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Titrate quetiapine 300 mg nocte as pharmacological maintenance for the mood instability she has been experiencing at present
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are not first line for borderline personality disorder without prominent psychotic or persistent affective symptoms; therapy is first line. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Start sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily to reduce impulsivity and stabilise reactive mood swings in coming months
options.rationale: Sodium valproate is not recommended first line for borderline personality disorder and carries teratogenic risk in a woman of childbearing potential. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Continue citalopram 20 mg and add clonazepam 0.5 mg as needed for distress spikes she has been experiencing lately
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines have a paradoxical disinhibiting risk in borderline personality disorder and increase self harm and overdose risk; not first line. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Refer for structured evidence based psychotherapy such as dialectical behaviour therapy or mentalisation based therapy
options.rationale: First line management of borderline personality disorder is a structured evidence based psychotherapy such as dialectical behaviour therapy, mentalisation based therapy, schema focused therapy or transference focused therapy; medications are not the primary treatment and are only used for comorbid conditions. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Inpatient admission for 6 weeks for stabilisation and observation regardless of current risk level at this early presentation
options.rationale: Long inpatient admission for borderline personality disorder is not evidence based and can worsen outcomes; brief crisis admission may be used but is not first line management. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

explanation.summary: Structured evidence based psychotherapy is first line for borderline personality disorder. Options include dialectical behaviour therapy, mentalisation based therapy, schema focused therapy and transference focused therapy. Medications are not first line; they are reserved for treating comorbid conditions such as a major depressive episode, an anxiety disorder or a substance use disorder. Benzodiazepines are avoided because of disinhibition and overdose risk. Brief admission may be indicated for acute suicidality but long term inpatient care worsens outcomes. Assertive community follow up between sessions supports engagement.
key_points: First line borderline personality disorder treatment is a structured psychotherapy: dialectical behaviour therapy, mentalisation based therapy, schema focused therapy or transference focused therapy.
Pharmacotherapy is reserved for treating comorbid conditions, not for the personality disorder itself.
Benzodiazepines carry disinhibition and overdose risk in this population.
explanation.pearls: Refer a woman with pure borderline personality disorder to dialectical behaviour therapy first; drug treatment is reserved for treating comorbid conditions.

sources.label: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder
RANZCP Guideline for Managing Borderline Personality Disorder

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose electrocardiogram threshold for sodium bicarbonate
stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar receiving a 34 year old woman by ambulance 90 minutes after a witnessed ingestion of a partner's amitriptyline. Her partner estimates 60 tablets of 25 mg were missing. She is now agitated, tachycardic, mildly hypotensive and has had one brief tonic clonic seizure at the scene lasting under 1 minute that terminated spontaneously. Ambulance gave 5 mg intravenous midazolam and 1 L 0.9 percent saline. She is protecting her airway.

Cardiac monitor shows a wide complex regular rhythm at 118 /min. A 12 lead electrocardiogram has been performed. Point of care glucose 6.2 mmol/L. She has been under continuous cardiac monitoring since arrival. There is no other co ingestion reported. Charcoal has not been given because of the delayed presentation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but arousable, dilated pupils reactive at 5 mm, dry mucous membranes, no clonus, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: 12 lead electrocardiogram: sinus tachycardia at 118 /min, terminal 40 ms axis R in aVR 5 mm, QRS 152 ms, QTc 480 ms; venous pH 7.32 lactate 3.0 mmol/L

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate intervention now?

options.text: Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg because midazolam given by ambulance may be contributing to her drowsiness on arrival
options.rationale: Flumazenil in a mixed overdose that includes a pro convulsant (tricyclic antidepressant) can precipitate seizure and arrhythmia; it is contraindicated in this setting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning

options.text: Intravenous physostigmine 2 mg because dilated pupils and dry mouth suggest a peripheral anticholinergic toxidrome now
options.rationale: Physostigmine is contraindicated in tricyclic antidepressant overdose because it can precipitate asystole; it is reserved for pure anticholinergic toxidromes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning

options.text: Intravenous amiodarone 300 mg for the broad complex tachycardia now visible on the cardiac monitor at present
options.rationale: Class III antiarrhythmics prolong QT and worsen tricyclic antidepressant cardiotoxicity; they are contraindicated in this setting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g bolus and observation only, with no other pharmacological intervention required now
options.rationale: Magnesium alone does not correct the sodium channel blockade responsible for QRS widening in tricyclic antidepressant overdose; sodium bicarbonate is the specific antidote. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 8.4 percent 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus over a few minutes then further boluses to QRS narrowing
options.rationale: Tricyclic antidepressant toxicity produces sodium channel blockade seen on the electrocardiogram as QRS >=100 ms (in particular >=120 ms) and a terminal R in aVR >=3 mm; the specific antidote is 8.4 percent sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg boluses titrated to QRS narrowing and reversal of hypotension, along with airway protection and seizure control. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose produces sodium channel blockade in the myocardium and central nervous system with anticholinergic, alpha adrenergic and gamma aminobutyric acid effects. Electrocardiogram markers of severe toxicity are QRS >=100 ms (particularly >=120 ms), a terminal R in aVR >=3 mm and rightward axis of the terminal 40 ms QRS vector. The antidote is 8.4 percent sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg boluses to a serum pH of 7.50 to 7.55 and QRS narrowing, plus airway support, benzodiazepines for seizure, and noradrenaline for refractory hypotension. Physostigmine, flumazenil and class I/III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated.
key_points: Toxic electrocardiogram markers: QRS >=100 ms (>=120 severe), terminal R in aVR >=3 mm.
Antidote: 8.4 percent sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus titrated to QRS and pH 7.50 to 7.55.
Avoid physostigmine, flumazenil, class I/III antiarrhythmics.
explanation.pearls: QRS 152 ms and R in aVR 5 mm in a tricyclic antidepressant overdose gets 1 to 2 mmol/kg 8.4 percent sodium bicarbonate boluses targeted to QRS narrowing.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning
Australian Poisons Information Centre Antidote Guidelines
